title: Arithmetic and Geometric Progression

references.label: GSSSB Laboratory Assistant Detailed Syllabus, Part A (Advt. 327/2025-26)

scientificNotes: General competitive-exam quantitative-aptitude topic; included to match the exam's Part A scope.
explanation: An Arithmetic Progression (AP) has a CONSTANT DIFFERENCE (d) between consecutive terms (added each step); a Geometric Progression (GP) has a CONSTANT RATIO (r) between consecutive terms (multiplied each step) — recognising which pattern a sequence follows (subtraction stays constant → AP; division stays constant → GP) is the first and most important step, since applying an AP formula to a GP sequence (or vice versa) gives a completely wrong answer. The nth-term formula finds any individual term directly without listing all preceding terms; the sum formula totals the first n terms directly without adding them one by one. For an INFINITE GP with |r| < 1 (a proper fraction), the terms shrink toward zero and the sum converges to a finite value: S∞ = a/(1−r) — this special case appears often in recurring-decimal-to-fraction conversions and certain physics/finance series problems.

variables.meaning: Common difference (AP) — constant amount added each step
Common ratio (GP) — constant factor multiplied each step
Term number / number of terms summed

workedExample.scenario: Find the sum of the first 10 terms of the AP 3, 7, 11, 15, ...

commonMistakes: Assuming every numeric sequence must be either an AP or a GP — some sequences follow entirely different rules (e.g. squares, alternating operations); always verify the constant-difference or constant-ratio property on at least 3 consecutive terms before applying either formula.
Using the GP sum formula a(rⁿ−1)/(r−1) when r = 1 — this formula is undefined (division by zero) at r = 1, where the sum is instead simply Sₙ = a×n (every term is identical).
genZNote: AP grows by addition, GP grows by multiplication — mixing up which one you're looking at is the fastest way to get a beautifully wrong answer.
